---
title: "Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?"
subtitle: "EVs are much cheaper to run. They're not cheaper to own, at least not new. Here's the math, per year."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-16"
categories: [cars, cost of living, energy]
image: infographic.png
---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/ev_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)

usd <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ","))
s_ev <- cost_row("Medium sedan", "Electric"); s_gas <- cost_row("Medium sedan", "Gas"); s_hy <- cost_row("Medium sedan", "Hybrid")
c_ev <- cost_row("Compact SUV", "Electric");  c_gas <- cost_row("Compact SUV", "Gas")
```

Electric car fans say you'll save a fortune on gas. Skeptics say EVs cost more and lose value fast. They're
both partly right. To settle it, we compared the **full cost of owning** an EV, a gas car, and a hybrid of the
**same size and class**, **per year**.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
An EV saves you about **`r usd(s_gas$running - s_ev$running)` a year** on fuel and maintenance (for a medium sedan).
But it loses value so much faster that a new EV costs **`r usd(s_ev$total_per_year - s_gas$total_per_year)` more per year**
to own than a comparable gas sedan. In SUVs, it's roughly a tie. And in every class, a **hybrid** was cheapest.
:::

## How we compared them

We used AAA's 2026 *Your Driving Costs* study, which averages the top-selling 2026 models in each class and
adds up everything it costs to own one for five years at 15,000 miles a year:

- **Fuel or charging**
- **Maintenance and repairs**, including tires
- **Depreciation**: how much value the car loses
- **Insurance** (full coverage)
- **License, registration, and taxes**, including the extra EV fees most states now charge
- **Finance charges**: interest on the car loan

That puts every vehicle on the same footing: **dollars per year.**

## The results

```{r total chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- ggplot(aaa, aes(total_per_year, fct_rev(class), fill = powertrain, group = fct_rev(powertrain),
                     text = paste0(class, " (", powertrain, "): ", usd(total_per_year), " per year"))) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Electric = "#2A9D8F", Gas = "#C53030", Hybrid = "#D69E2E")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Total cost per year (15,000 miles)", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

```{r total table}
aaa %>%
  select(class, powertrain, total_per_year) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = powertrain, values_from = total_per_year) %>%
  mutate(`EV vs gas` = ifelse(Electric > Gas, paste0("EV costs ", usd(Electric - Gas), " more"),
                              paste0("EV saves ", usd(Gas - Electric))),
         across(c(Electric, Gas, Hybrid), usd)) %>%
  rename(Class = class) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrl", caption = "Total cost per year, new 2026 models, 15,000 miles a year. Source: AAA.")
```

## Where EVs win: running costs

The EV advantage is real. For a medium sedan, charging cost about **`r usd(s_ev$fuel)` a year** versus
**`r usd(s_gas$fuel)`** for gas, and maintenance was cheaper too (no oil changes, fewer moving parts, and brakes
that last longer thanks to regenerative braking).

```{r running chart}
#| fig-height: 4
running <- aaa %>%
  select(class, powertrain, Fuel = fuel, Maintenance = maintenance) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Fuel, Maintenance), names_to = "cost", values_to = "dollars")

p2 <- ggplot(running, aes(dollars, powertrain, fill = cost, text = paste0(class, ", ", powertrain, " - ", cost, ": ", usd(dollars)))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~class, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Fuel = "#1F4E5A", Maintenance = "#7FE0CF")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Fuel + maintenance per year", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.12)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

**One big catch: where you charge.** AAA's EV fuel costs line up with home electricity prices, which average
about **$`r round(home_kwh_price, 2)` per kWh** nationally. Public fast chargers typically cost around
**$`r public_kwh_price` per kWh**, about **`r round(public_multiplier, 1)` times** more. If you can't charge at home
and rely on fast chargers, a medium sedan's charging bill rises to roughly
**`r usd(s_ev$fuel * public_multiplier)` a year**: still less than gas, but most of the savings are gone.

## Where EVs lose: owning costs

```{r owning chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
owning <- aaa %>%
  filter(powertrain != "Hybrid") %>%
  select(class, powertrain, Depreciation = depreciation, Insurance = insurance,
         `Registration & taxes` = registration_taxes, `Loan interest` = finance) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(class, powertrain), names_to = "cost", values_to = "dollars") %>%
  mutate(cost = factor(cost, levels = c("Depreciation", "Insurance", "Registration & taxes", "Loan interest")))

p3 <- ggplot(owning, aes(dollars, powertrain, fill = cost, text = paste0(class, ", ", powertrain, " - ", cost, ": ", usd(dollars)))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~class, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Depreciation" = "#C53030", "Insurance" = "#D69E2E",
                               "Registration & taxes" = "#6C8BA8", "Loan interest" = "grey60")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Ownership costs per year", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

ggplotly(p3, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.12)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The biggest single cost of owning *any* new car is **depreciation**, the value it loses while you own it. For
EVs, it's brutal. AAA puts a new electric medium sedan's depreciation at **`r usd(s_ev$depreciation)` a year**, versus
**`r usd(s_gas$depreciation)`** for gas. Fast-improving battery technology and price cuts on new EVs make used
ones worth less.

EVs also tend to cost more to **insure** (they're pricier to repair), most states now charge an extra
**annual EV registration fee** (often $100 to $250) to make up for lost gas-tax revenue, and a pricier car means
more **loan interest**. And as of September 30, 2025, the **$7,500 federal EV tax credit is gone**.

## So who should buy an EV?

The numbers point to a few clear cases where an EV makes financial sense:

- **You can charge at home.** That's where the fuel savings come from.
- **You drive a lot.** More miles means more fuel savings to offset the extra ownership costs.
- **You keep cars a long time.** Depreciation is heaviest in the first few years. Keep the car 10 years
  and the per-year cost of that early drop shrinks.
- **You buy used.** The first owner already took the big depreciation hit. A used EV can capture the
  running-cost savings without paying for the steepest part of the value drop.
- **You're shopping SUVs, not sedans.** The gap is smallest there.

If saving money is the top priority and none of those fit, the data say: **buy a hybrid.** It beat both EVs
and gas cars in every class AAA measured.

## The fine print

- **These are averages** across top-selling models. A specific EV with a big discount, or a gas guzzler, can
  change the answer.
- **Five-year ownership** is AAA's assumption. Longer ownership generally helps EVs.
- **Electricity and gas prices vary a lot by state.** Cheap power and expensive gas favor EVs.
- **Public charging prices** vary by network and membership; ours is a typical 2026 figure.
- This post is about money. **Whether EVs are better for the environment** is a separate question, and our
  follow-up post tackles it.

## The bottom line

EVs really are cheaper to run. But "cheaper to run" isn't "cheaper to own." Buying new, without the old
federal tax credit, an EV costs about the same as a gas SUV and more than a gas sedan, because it loses value so
fast. If you can charge at home, drive a lot, keep cars for years, or buy used, the math tilts toward electric.
Otherwise, a hybrid is the money winner.

---

**How we did this.** Annual costs are from AAA's *Your Driving Costs* 2026 study (EV, gas, and hybrid
comparison for medium sedans, compact SUVs, medium SUVs, and pickups; 15,000 miles a year, five-year ownership,
full-coverage insurance). Home electricity is the BLS average U.S. price per kWh over the last 12 months, via
[FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/APU000072610). The public fast-charging price is a typical 2026 figure from
industry price trackers.
